opus-5.5.text:
I think the first thing is to be honest about what six months actually means. It sounds like a lot of time, but once you subtract running experiments, debugging, writing, and the rebuttal cycle, the window for genuinely thinking about *what* to do is quite small. So a lot of people panic and pick whatever is closest at hand, usually some incremental tweak on the paper that just came out. I understand why, but I think that's often the least efficient choice, because ten other groups are looking at the same paper and having the same idea that same week.

What I try to do, and what I tell my students, is to separate the idea from the deadline. The idea should come from something you've been carrying around for a long time, a question that keeps bothering you, something that feels a little bit wrong about how the field is doing things. The six-month cycle is just the vehicle for testing one slice of that bigger question. If you only start thinking when the cycle starts, you're already late.

Second, I really value ideas that come from looking closely at things yourself. Not reading the abstract, but actually running the baseline, looking at the failure cases, visualizing the features, staring at the data. Very often the interesting idea is hiding in some small observation that doesn't match your expectation. When I worked on things like ResNeXt or ConvNeXt, a lot of it was just being stubborn about checking assumptions everyone took for granted. Like, is this design choice actually necessary, or did we just inherit it? That kind of question is cheap to ask and sometimes leads somewhere surprising.

Third, I think you need some taste about risk. I like to have a project where the core bet is a little bit bold, but structured so that even if the bold version doesn't fully work, you learn something real along the way. Pure safe ideas give you a paper but not much else. Pure moonshots in six months often give you nothing, and that's very hard on a young researcher's confidence.

And finally, talk to people. A lot of my best ideas got sharper, or got killed quickly, which is equally valuable, because I explained them to someone over coffee and they asked one annoying question. Killing a bad idea in week two is a huge win. The worst outcome isn't a failed idea, it's spending five months on something you could have known was wrong in the first two weeks.

So in short: carry long-term questions, look at things with your own eyes, take calibrated risks, and get feedback early. The deadline is real, but it shouldn't be the thing deciding what you work on.

r001.rationale: The response advises carrying a long-term question or broader research concern before the six-month cycle begins, which communicates an initial general research direction.

r002.rationale: It says the time for thinking during the cycle is small and advises starting earlier, but does not recommend reserving one to two months for exploration.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, because six months is actually a very awkward window. It's long enough that you can't just chase whatever came out on arXiv last week, but it's short enough that you can't afford to wander for three months and then panic.

The first thing I'd say is that the idea doesn't come from sitting down and saying "I need an idea." It comes from a longer-running sense of what you believe about the field. For me, a lot of the work I've done comes from a few fairly stubborn convictions, like the belief that simple, scalable architectures tend to win in the long run, or that the vision community sometimes borrows from language models without asking whether the borrowed piece is actually the important one. If you have one or two convictions like that, then finding a six-month project is really just asking: what's the smallest, cleanest experiment that would test this conviction or push it one step further?

The second thing is that I'd encourage people, especially students, to start from a question rather than a method. "Can we make this architecture faster" is a method-first framing, and it usually leads to incremental work. "Why does this thing work at all" or "what happens if we remove the part everyone assumes is necessary" are question-first framings. Those tend to produce results that are interesting even if the answer is negative, which matters a lot when you only have six months and can't guarantee the outcome.

Third, be very honest about the risk profile early. In the first few weeks I think you should run the ugliest, fastest version of the experiment you can, almost deliberately sloppy, just to see if the signal is there. A lot of people spend two months building infrastructure before they learn anything. If the crude version shows nothing, that's incredibly valuable information at week three rather than week twenty.

And finally, talk to people. Not to get the idea from them, but because explaining a half-formed idea out loud is the fastest way to discover whether you actually believe it. If you can't make it sound interesting to a colleague in five minutes, it's usually not that the colleague is missing something, it's that the idea isn't sharp enough yet. Sharpening it is most of the work. The experiments are almost the easy part after that.

r001.rationale: The response says idea-finding starts from a longer-running sense of what you believe about the field and one or two convictions, which communicates an initial general research direction.

r002.rationale: The response does not recommend reserving one to two months for exploration; it instead warns against wandering for three months and recommends testing a crude experiment in the first few weeks.

astra-6.text:
I think the first thing is to avoid treating those six months as a deadline for having a great idea. You can plan experiments, but it’s hard to schedule insight. What you can do is create a process that gives you more chances to find something interesting.

I would start with a question that you genuinely want to understand, even if it’s still a little vague. Then get into experiments fairly quickly. Reproduce something, build a simple baseline, and look closely at where your expectations don’t match the results. Often, the useful idea comes from that mismatch. You thought something should work, it didn’t, and now you have a more specific question.

The balance is between giving a direction enough time and being willing to let it go. If you switch every week, you never understand anything deeply. But if you spend five months defending your original intuition, you may miss what the experiments are telling you. I’d periodically ask: What have we learned? Is the question getting clearer? What experiment would actually change our mind?

So within a six-month cycle, I’d focus less on finding the perfect idea at the beginning and more on making steady progress toward a clear question and convincing evidence. The initial idea is a starting point. It doesn’t have to be the final contribution.

r001.rationale: The candidate recommends starting with a question the researcher wants to understand, even if it is vague, which communicates an initial general research direction.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not recommend reserving one to two months, or any specific portion of the six-month cycle, for exploration.

sol-6.1.text:
I think six months is a useful planning horizon, but finding an idea doesn’t really follow a fixed schedule. You can’t say, “I’ll spend the first month having the idea, then five months executing it.” Often, the idea becomes clear only after you start doing experiments.

I would start with a question you care about and ask: what is the smallest experiment that could tell me whether there’s something here? You want to get into that feedback loop quickly. Even if the result is negative, understanding why can give you a much better question.

The tricky part is balancing persistence with being willing to change direction. If something doesn’t work, that alone isn’t a reason to stop. But you should be learning something. If you’ve spent weeks running experiments and your understanding hasn’t changed, it’s probably time to step back and revisit the premise.

So I wouldn’t optimize for finding one perfect idea at the beginning. I’d optimize for learning quickly enough that, over those six months, an initially vague intuition can become a clear, well-supported contribution.

r001.rationale: The response recommends starting with a question you care about, but does not state that searching for an idea requires an initial general research direction.

r002.rationale: It discusses learning through experiments over six months but does not recommend reserving one to two months for exploration.
